t: The LORD, and the word that came
p: The divine name YHWH is written "the LORD" in this Plain; the book opens as the Twelve open.
b: The Hebrew has the four letters YHWH, the personal name of Israel's God, which Jewish readers did not say aloud and which most English Bibles print as "the LORD" in capitals. "The word of the LORD that came to" is the standard opening of a prophet's book (Hosea 1:1; Joel 1:1; Micah 1:1). Zephaniah's opening is the most carefully dated of the Twelve: it names four generations of his family and then the king of the day. Compare the shorter openings of Obadiah and Habakkuk, which name neither father nor king.

a: Zephaniah son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hezekiah
p: No other prophet's family is traced this far back; "Hezekiah" may be the king, and "Cushi" means "the Cushite."
b: Zephaniah is the only prophet whose family is traced back four generations. The name means "the LORD has hidden" or "treasured." His father's name, Cushi, is the Hebrew word for "a Cushite" (a man of Nubia, south of Egypt); it is a name in Jeremiah 36:14 too. Why trace the line to a Hezekiah? Some think this is King Hezekiah (about 715 to 686 BC), which would make Zephaniah a distant cousin of Josiah. The Hebrew does not say "king," while it does for Josiah, so others think the ancestor is a different man, perhaps named to show that a man with a foreign-sounding family was a true Israelite. Others think the name only records a Cushite connection somewhere in the family. The text does not decide.

a: in the days of Josiah son of Amon
p: Zephaniah speaks in Josiah's reign (640 to 609 BC); whether before or after the reform of 622 is the first question.
b: Josiah became king at eight, after servants killed his father Amon (2 Kings 21:19-24; 22:1). In his eighth year he began to seek God, in his twelfth year he began to clean up Judah and Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 34:3), and in his eighteenth year (about 622 BC) the law-book was found in the Temple and the great reform followed (2 Kings 22:3-23:25). He died at Megiddo in 609, meeting Pharaoh Neco (2 Kings 23:29). Zephaniah's words about Baal, the idol priests and the star-worshipers on the roofs (1:4-5) suit the years before the reform, and that is the commonest dating. Others place the book during or after the reform, or think later writers reworked it. See the book introduction.

p: The Hebrew opens with two forms of one verb, asoph asef, which can mean gather in or sweep away.
b: The verse begins with the same verb twice, an infinitive and a first-person form: asoph asef. The verb asaf usually means "gather" (a harvest, a crowd, the dead "gathered" to their people) and it can also mean "take away, bring to an end" (1 Samuel 15:6; Jeremiah 8:13). The doubling makes it strong: a complete end, a total harvest of everything. The verb comes back, turned the other way, when the LORD says he will "gather" the scattered (3:18-20). Verse 18 ends the chapter with another word for finishing, kalah, "a complete end."

a: off the surface of the ground
p: "From the surface of the ground" is the wording of the flood story, where God wipes out life on the ground.
b: The Hebrew says 'adamah, "ground," not 'erets, "earth." That is the word of the flood: God says he will wipe from "the surface of the ground" every living thing he made (Genesis 6:7; Genesis 7:4). Zephaniah 1:2-3 is built on the flood. After the flood God promised never again to strike down every living thing (Genesis 8:21; Genesis 9:11), so readers have asked whether Zephaniah breaks that promise or speaks in sweeping poetry about a coming disaster for Judah. The Plain keeps "ground" so the link with Adam in verse 3 can be heard.

p: The Hebrew ne'um YHWH is a noun phrase, "an utterance of the LORD," and closes many prophetic lines.
b: Ne'um is a noun, "an utterance," so the phrase means "the LORD's utterance." It is a signature the prophets put at the end of a saying, a claim that the words come from God. Zephaniah has it in 1:2, 3, 10; 2:9 and 3:8 (where it comes in the middle of a verse) and the Plain gives it as "the LORD declares" set off by commas, as in Kings and Jeremiah. The shorter "the LORD says" (3:20) renders a different Hebrew verb.

a: I will end people and animals.
t: A sweep of the whole earth, or of Judah's land?
p: Read literally, the line is world judgment; others read it as sweeping language for a disaster on Judah.
b: Taken at its word, 1:2-3 announces the end of every living thing, the flood undone. Four readings are common. (1) World judgment: the book uses "earth" and "all who live on the earth" (1:18; 3:8), and the nations are judged in chapter 2. (2) Hyperbole for Judah: the same sweeping words are used of a land laid waste (Jeremiah 4:23-26; Hosea 4:3), and Judah's land is the target in 1:4. (3) The last judgment: Christian and Jewish readers have read it as the end of the age. (4) A later opening: some critics think an editor placed a universal frame around the oracles on Judah. The Plain translates the words as they stand.

a: the birds of the sky and the fish of the sea
p: Zephaniah lists people, animals, birds, fish: the order of Genesis 1, backwards.
b: Genesis 1 makes sea creatures and birds on the fifth day, then land animals and humans on the sixth (Genesis 1:20-27). Zephaniah lists the victims in the opposite order: people and animals, birds, fish. The same reversal of creation appears in Jeremiah 4:23-26, where the earth goes back to "shapeless and empty" and the birds are gone, and in Hosea 4:3, where animals, birds and fish waste away. The line is a way of saying that judgment undoes what the Creator built. The Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus, drops the "stumbling blocks" and turns the end of the verse into a judgment on the lawless (see the variant).

p: The Hebrew word occurs only here and in Isaiah 3:6; it can mean ruins or things that make people fall.
b: Makhshelot comes from the root "stumble." The Hebrew has three meanings in play. Things that make people fall into sin, especially idols (Ezekiel 14:3-7 uses a related word for idols that are "a stumbling block of guilt"). Heaps of ruins, as in Isaiah 3:6, "this heap of ruins" (a related form), which is how some translations take it. Or the verb "the wicked will stumble," which is how the Greek reads it. The Plain keeps the literal "stumbling blocks," which allows both the idol and the ruin senses, and sits "together with the wicked."

p: Hebrew plays on 'adam (humankind) and 'adamah (ground): people cut off from the ground they were made from.
b: "Humankind" is ha'adam, and "the ground" is ha'adamah. In Genesis 2:7 the first human is formed from the ground, and Genesis 3:19 says he will return to it. Here the sound-play runs the other way: the human race will be cut off from the very ground it came from. The Plain's "humankind" and "ground" keep the near-echo in English. The verse is also the one place where the Greek says something else: not "cut off humankind" but "remove the lawless" (see the variant).

a: I will reach out my hand against Judah
p: "Reach out the hand" is the old language for God's mighty act of judgment; the target narrows to Judah.
b: The phrase natah yad 'al is used of God's power at the exodus (Exodus 7:5) and of his judging hand against Israel itself (Isaiah 5:25; Jeremiah 6:12; Ezekiel 6:14). After the sweep over "the ground" (1:2-3) the camera drops to a single kingdom and a single city: Judah and Jerusalem. Readers who see 1:2-3 as universal take this as the first example; readers who see 1:2-3 as poetic overstatement take it as the real target all along.

p: The Hebrew word is used of priests of false gods; it appears only here, in Hosea 10:5 and in 2 Kings 23:5.
b: Kemarim (singular komer) appears only three times in the Bible: here, in Hosea 10:5, for the priests of the calf at Beth-aven, and in 2 Kings 23:5, where Josiah removes the "idol priests" the kings of Judah had put in place to burn incense at the high places. The word is related to Akkadian and Aramaic words for priest, and the Syriac kumra means a priest, often a pagan one. The Plain uses "idol priests" in all three. Zephaniah sets them next to "the priests," which suggests priests of the LORD who served alongside them or were compromised (see 1:5).

p: To cut off a name is to wipe out memory of it; Hosea and Zechariah use the same threat against idols.
b: In the Bible a name is the way a person or god is remembered and worshiped. To "cut off the name" is to end the worship so completely that the name is forgotten. Hosea 2:17 has the LORD say he will take the names of the Baals from Israel's mouth, and Zechariah 13:2 says he will cut off the names of the idols so they are no longer remembered. The Septuagint reads "the names of Baal" in the first half of the verse (see the variant), which makes the same point.

p: Flat roofs were used for burning incense to the stars; Josiah tore down roof altars.
b: The flat roofs of houses were open, high places of their own, and a good place to watch the sky. Jeremiah says the people burned incense to "all the army of the heavens" on their rooftops (Jeremiah 19:13; 32:29). When Josiah cleaned up the Temple he pulled down the altars on the roof of Ahaz's upper room (2 Kings 23:12). On the roof the worshiper could face the stars, with nothing between him and them. Zephaniah's verse is one of the best evidence for a private, household astral cult in Judah in the 600s BC, separate from the Temple's official worship.

p: The sun, moon and stars worshiped as gods; the Bible calls them an "army" that belongs to the LORD.
b: Tseva hashamayim is the army of the sky: the stars, with sun and moon, thought of as living powers who march at God's command (Genesis 2:1; Isaiah 40:26). Moses warned Israel not to bow to them (Deuteronomy 4:19; 17:3). King Manasseh built altars for the whole army of the heavens in both courtyards of the Temple (2 Kings 21:3-5), and Josiah removed them (2 Kings 23:4-5, 12). Whether Assyria forced this star-worship on its vassals, or Judah took it up itself, scholars debate; many recent scholars hold that Judah adopted it freely. The phrase "LORD of Armies" (2:9) uses the same word: the armies belong to him.

a: those who bow down and swear oaths to the LORD
t: Worship of the LORD mixed with other gods
p: Zephaniah names people who keep faith with the LORD and with another god at once.
b: These worshipers do not abandon the LORD. They bow down to him and swear oaths in his name, which the law allows (Deuteronomy 6:13; 10:20), and they also swear by another god. Scholars call this syncretism, a blend. Zephaniah calls it a betrayal. Amos had the same charge against those who swore by the guilt of Samaria and by the way of Beersheba (Amos 8:14), and Jeremiah against people who swore by false gods in the same breath as the LORD (Jeremiah 5:7). The charge is not that the LORD is ignored, but that he is made one among several.

a: backed away from following the LORD
p: The Hebrew verb nasog means to retreat or fall back; it is the opposite of turning back to God.
b: The verb nasog means to draw back, fall away, retreat. It is used of a heart that has not turned back (Psalm 44:18) and of people turning away from following our God (Isaiah 59:13). The Hebrew phrase "from after the LORD" pictures a follower who stops walking behind his leader. The word is near in meaning to Jeremiah's "turning away" (meshuvah), the backslider (Jeremiah 3:6-14). A reader who knows the Hebrew verb shuv, "turn," hears the other side in Zephaniah: these people have not turned toward God, but away.

p: Two verbs, baqash (seek) and darash (inquire, consult), are used for turning to God; 2:3 asks for them again.
b: Baqash means to look for; darash means to inquire, to consult someone, as a person asks a prophet or a priest. Together they describe a life oriented toward God: asking what he wants, looking for his help. Amos 5:4-6 puts it as a command, "Seek me and live." Zephaniah 1:6 names the people who have done neither. The word "seek" returns in 2:3 as the prophet's one hope: "Seek the LORD... seek righteousness... seek humility." Chapter 1 shows the people who do not seek; chapter 2 begins by asking them to.

p: The Hebrew has has, a sound for silence; Habakkuk 2:20 and Zechariah 2:13 use the same word.
b: Has is an imitation of a hush. It is a command to stop talking, the way a crowd goes quiet when a judge stands up, or when a funeral begins (Amos 6:10, where a survivor says the same hush so the name of the LORD is not spoken). The same sound is used in Habakkuk 2:20, "Hush before him, all the earth," and Zechariah 2:13. The editor of the Twelve may have placed Zephaniah next to Habakkuk on purpose. The "Lord GOD" in capital letters is Adonai YHWH, "my Lord, the LORD."
orig: הַס מִפְּנֵי אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה (has mippenei adonay YHWH)

a: The LORD has prepared a sacrifice
p: The "sacrifice" is the slaughter of Judah; the invited guests are those who carry it out.
b: The prophets use the image of a sacrificial meal for a slaughter of people. Isaiah 34:6 says the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, in Edom's land. Jeremiah 46:10 says the Lord GOD of Armies has a sacrifice by the Euphrates. Ezekiel 39:17-20 calls the birds and beasts to feast on a sacrifice on the mountains of Israel. Revelation 19:17-18 has the same picture. In each, the victims are the guilty and the guests are the scavengers or the army that brings the end. Zephaniah's twist is that the victim is Judah, God's own people.

a: He has made holy the ones he invited.
p: The invited, "made holy" guests are most often taken to be the army that comes against Jerusalem.
b: A holy meal needs holy guests. Three readings. (1) The Babylonian army, set apart for war the way soldiers were "made holy" before battle (Isaiah 13:3, "my holy ones"; Jeremiah 6:4, "make holy war"); this is the commonest view. (2) The birds and beasts who eat the dead, as in Ezekiel 39:17. (3) The people of Judah themselves, invited like worshipers to a sacrifice and found to be the sacrifice, as 1:8 may imply. The Greek reads "he has made holy his called ones," close to the Hebrew.

t: The royal family under a boy king
p: Josiah's own sons were not yet born in his first years, so "the king's sons" may mean the royal house in general.
b: Josiah was eight when he became king (2 Kings 22:1). His sons Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim were 23 and 25 when they took the throne in 609 (2 Kings 23:31, 36), so they were born only after he had reigned some years. If Zephaniah spoke in Josiah's first years, "the king's sons" cannot mean Josiah's children. The phrase can mean any prince of the royal family (compare Jeremiah 36:26). The "officials" would then be the court that ruled for the boy. A later date would allow Josiah's actual sons. Who the powerful men of the time were is part of the evidence for the book's date.

p: The clothes show allegiance to foreign culture or foreign gods; Israelites were told to mark their clothes as their own.
b: Clothing was a flag. Israelites were told to put tassels on their garments to remind them of the LORD's commands (Numbers 15:37-41). Foreign clothes could mean the fashions of Assyria, the great power whose style Judah's court copied, or special garments worn for the rites of another god (2 Kings 10:22 mentions robes given to Baal's worshipers). In either case the sin is not fashion. It is divided loyalty, declared on the body. Zephaniah's first targets are the powerful: the officials and the royal house.

p: Two ancient readings: a ritual avoidance of the doorsill, or a violent raid into houses.
b: When the ark of the LORD had been in the Philistine temple, the priests of Dagon would not step on the doorsill of Dagon's house, "down to this day" (1 Samuel 5:5). Some read Zephaniah's "leap over the doorsill" the same way: a pagan custom, imported to Judah, of leaping a threshold where a spirit was thought to live. Others read it as people who leap into the houses of others to rob them and fill their masters' houses with the plunder. The "masters" are then the powerful officials, or perhaps the false gods. The Greek has a different text here (see the variant).

p: A gate on the north side of Jerusalem, near the fish market; an invader from the north would reach it first.
b: The Fish Gate stood in the northern wall of Jerusalem. Manasseh's outer wall reached it (2 Chronicles 33:14), and Nehemiah's rebuilders worked on it (Nehemiah 3:3; 12:39). Nehemiah 13:16 tells of men from Tyre who sold fish there. The three sounds of this verse, a cry at the Fish Gate, a howl from the Second District and a great shattering from the hills, trace the attack as it moves inward from the north: gate, new quarter, the hills of the old city.

p: The Hebrew hamishneh, "the second," is a newer part of Jerusalem; the prophet Huldah lived there.
b: Hamishneh means "the second" and is a district of Jerusalem. It was the home of the prophet Huldah when Josiah's men came to ask her about the law-book (2 Kings 22:14). Nehemiah calls a man "second over the city" in a related use (Nehemiah 11:9). The district is usually placed on the western hill. Digging in today's Jewish Quarter found a thick wall, the "Broad Wall," that shows the city had spread west by the late 700s BC, a growth often explained by the refugees who came south after Samaria fell.

p: A hollow in Jerusalem where merchants worked; the Hebrew word means a mortar.
b: Hammakhtesh means "the mortar," a bowl-shaped hollow. Proverbs 27:22 uses it for the stone bowl in which grain is pounded. Here it is a district of Jerusalem, and the context, "the people of Canaan," "all who weigh out silver," shows it was the market. Its exact place is unknown. It is often put in the valley that ran through the middle of the city (the Tyropoeon, or Central Valley), where a market in a bowl-shaped hollow would be handy to both hills.

p: "Canaanite" also meant "merchant" in Hebrew, and here the traders of Jerusalem are called Canaan.
b: In Hebrew kena'ani, "Canaanite," could mean a trader, because the Phoenician coast was home to the great merchants. Hosea 12:7 says "Canaan" has scales of deceit in his hand, and Proverbs 31:24 uses the word for a seller. The Plain keeps "people of Canaan" so the reader hears the double meaning: these are the merchants of Jerusalem, and the prophet is calling them by the name of the people Israel was told to drive out. "Weigh out silver" fits: money was weighed, not counted, before coins were common.

p: The Hebrew means those lifted up or weighed down with silver; the Greek reads "lifted up with silver."
b: Netile kesef literally means "those lifted (weighed) with silver." The root natal means to lift or to weigh. Most translations take the phrase as "those who weigh out silver," meaning dealers. The Greek reads "those lifted up with silver" (the wealthy), which supports taking it as "loaded down with silver." The Plain follows this because it fits both: the rich are the dealers.

p: No one can hide from a search with lamps, house by house; the Talmud uses this verse for the search for leaven.
b: Lamps carried through a dark city to find the hidden: the picture is a house-to-house search, in which no cellar or corner is skipped. Jeremiah 5:1 shows the same idea, a search through the streets of Jerusalem for one honest person. Amos 9:2-3 says no one escapes the LORD, even in the depths. In Jewish practice the Talmud cites this verse in explaining why the search for leaven before Passover is done by lamplight (Bavli Pesachim 7b-8a). Whether the verse is the main proof there or one of several, the lamp of Zephaniah became the lamp of the household search.

p: Wine that is never poured off thickens and turns sluggish; the image is of comfortable, unchallenged people.
b: Wine was left on the dregs to build flavor and then poured from jar to jar. Wine left too long on the dregs goes thick and stale. The Hebrew verb qapha is used of water that freezes or thickens (Exodus 15:8, "congealed"). Jeremiah 48:11 uses the same picture for Moab, "sitting still on his dregs," never poured into another jar and never sent into exile. Zephaniah's complacent men have gone thick in their ways, and the LORD says he will hunt them out with lamps. The Greek reads "despising their guards," taking the Hebrew word for "dregs" as a different noun.

a: The LORD will do no good, and he will do no harm.
p: A creed of a God who does not act: not unbelief in God, but unbelief that he will do anything.
b: These men do not deny that the LORD exists. They deny that he does anything. The same attitude is in Psalm 10:4, 11 ("God does not see"), in Jeremiah 5:12 (the people say he will do nothing and no harm will come to them), and Malachi 2:17. Scholars call this practical atheism. Isaiah 41:23 shows the root of the idea: a challenge to idols to "do good or do harm," which is the test of a living god. By saying the LORD can do neither, these men have made him no better than an idol. The prophet's answer is the whole next section: the LORD will act, and soon.

a: They will build houses and not live in them.
p: The covenant curses: build, plant, and never enjoy it; Amos and Micah use the same threat.
b: The line comes from the list of curses for breaking the covenant (Deuteronomy 28:30, 39). Amos 5:11 uses it against those who "build houses of cut stone" and will not live in them, and Micah 6:15 against those who plant and do not reap. The curse is a reversal of Israel's ideal peace, in which each family sits under its vine (1 Kings 4:25; Micah 4:4). The same Hebrew pattern runs through the Twelve: the sin that earned the curse is named, and the curse falls as the law said it would.

a: Close is the great day of the LORD
p: The day of the LORD, expected as victory, is turned into a day of defeat; Zephaniah gathers its older images.
b: The earliest use is Amos 5:18-20, where "Woe to you who long for the day of the LORD" meets a popular hope that the day would mean light for Israel. Isaiah 2:12 and 13:6-9, Joel 1:15 and 2:1-2, Obadiah 15 and Ezekiel 30:3 follow. Zephaniah is the longest sustained description and gives the day its heaviest weight. Scholars debate where the idea comes from: von Rad traced it to holy war, when the LORD fought for Israel; Mowinckel to a yearly festival of the LORD's kingship; others to a popular hope that God would act for his own people. Zephaniah uses the images of all of them. See the topic page.
r: Amos 5:18-20; Isaiah 13:6-9; Joel 1:15; Joel 2:1-2; Obadiah 15; Ezekiel 30:3

p: Who is the warrior? The LORD himself, a soldier of the day or a hero crying out; the word returns in 3:17.
b: Gibbor means a mighty fighter. The sentence is hard: "there" the warrior "cries out" (in pain or in the battle shout). Three readings. The warrior is a human hero, the best soldier of Judah, reduced to crying out in the hour of defeat. He is the invading soldier, shouting as he attacks. Or he is the LORD himself, who goes out "like a warrior" (Isaiah 42:13). In 3:17 the same word comes back: "a warrior who rescues." The book that opens with a warrior shouting ends with a warrior who rescues, rejoicing over her.

a: That day is a day of fury
p: The Latin of this verse, "dies irae, dies illa," opens the great hymn of the Requiem Mass.
b: In the Latin Bible (Jerome's Vulgate) Zephaniah 1:15 begins dies irae, dies illa, "a day of wrath, that day." Those words open the medieval Latin sequence sung at funeral Masses, the Dies irae, which pictures the last judgment: trumpet, book, the judge who sits. It is usually attributed to Thomas of Celano, a Franciscan of the 1200s, though the attribution is uncertain. Composers including Mozart and Verdi set it. The 1969 reform of the funeral rite removed it as the Requiem sequence; the 1962 Missal keeps it, and the Liturgy of the Hours uses it divided into three hymns. The hymn takes Zephaniah's day as the last day, a reading the prophet's own words do not make, but one the Latin church made its own. See the topic page.

a: a day of darkness and gloom
p: These words are also in Joel 2:2; Sinai, the plague of darkness and Amos 5:18 stand behind them.
b: Zephaniah's list uses the same pair of words as Joel 2:2, "a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and deep darkness," so either one used the other or both used a stock phrase. The images come from the exodus and Sinai: the plague of darkness (Exodus 10:21-22) and the mountain wrapped in darkness, cloud and deep darkness when the LORD spoke (Deuteronomy 4:11). Amos 5:18-20 says the day of the LORD is darkness, not light. The day of the LORD is then like Sinai, but now turned against Israel itself.

p: The Hebrew 'evrah means rage that overflows its banks; the Plain uses "fury."
b: 'Evrah comes from a root meaning to cross over or overflow, so "outburst" or "overflow of anger." The Hebrew language has several words for God's anger, and the Plain keeps them apart: 'af "anger," charon 'af "burning anger" (2:2; 3:8), 'evrah "fury" (1:15, 18), za'am "indignation" (3:8), qin'ah "jealousy" (1:18; 3:8). See the topic wrath for the whole group.

a: the ram's horn and the battle cry
p: Shofar and teru'ah: the signals of war; Amos, Joel and Hosea use the same pair.
b: The shofar is the ram's horn, a signal for alarm and for gathering for war. Teru'ah is the shout of battle or of joy. Amos 2:2 uses both together against Moab. Joel 2:1 says to blow the horn in Zion to warn of the day. In 3:14 the same root rua', "shout," returns as the call to joy: Israel will raise a shout, but this time of celebration. The same Hebrew sound is first battle cry, then song.

p: The Hebrew pinnot means corners; towers on the walls, or, in older language, the chiefs of a people.
b: Pinnah is a corner; it can mean a corner tower on a city wall (2 Chronicles 26:15 says Uzziah built towers at the corners). In older Hebrew the same word is also used of the "cornerstones" of a people, its chiefs (Judges 20:2; 1 Samuel 14:38; Isaiah 19:13). So "the high corner towers" may be a picture of the defenses or a hint at the leaders. The word returns in 3:6, "their corner towers lie in ruins."

p: The curse of blindness from Deuteronomy 28 is part of the day.
b: The covenant curses include being driven to grope "at noon" like a blind man in darkness (Deuteronomy 28:28-29). Isaiah 59:10 and Lamentations 4:14 use the picture of groping, stumbling people. The blindness here is the result of the "distress" the LORD brings, because the people have sinned against him. The verse names the reason in the middle of the line: not because Judah is weak, but because it "sinned against the LORD."

a: by the fire of his jealousy
p: God's jealousy is the fierce loyalty of a spouse; it is the sin of idolatry that sets it burning.
b: Qin'ah is the heat of zeal or jealousy. The second commandment says the LORD is a jealous God (Exodus 20:5), and Deuteronomy 4:24 calls him a consuming fire, a jealous God. The word is used of a husband's anger at a rival, so its use for God fits the marriage picture of the covenant (Hosea 1-3). Here it is the reason for the whole chapter: the idol worship of 1:4-6 is a rival to the LORD. The same phrase is repeated, with "my" for "his," in 3:8.
r: Exodus 20:5; Deuteronomy 4:24; Song of Songs 8:6; Zephaniah 3:8

a: The whole earth will be eaten up
p: "The whole earth" can be the whole world or the whole land of Judah, and the book is read both ways.
b: Kol ha'arets means "all the earth" or "all the land." The context decides: 1:2-3 spoke of the ground, 1:18 of "everyone who lives on the earth," and 3:8 repeats the sentence and speaks of nations. Readers who take the book as about Judah's fall (the preterist reading) translate "land" and treat it as grand speech for a regional catastrophe. Readers who take it as final judgment (the futurist reading) take "earth" literally. Both agree that the sentence is placed to close the chapter and returns at 3:8 to close the oracles on the nations. The Plain says "earth."

p: The Hebrew verb is built on qash, "straw"; people are told to gather themselves like gleaners.
b: The two verbs, hitqoshshu vaqoshu, come from qash, "straw, stubble," and the plain verb means to gather straw or sticks (Numbers 15:32, a man "gathering wood"; Exodus 5:7, 12). The Hebrew sounds like a clatter of dry sticks. The call may mean "pick yourselves over, as gleaners do": examine yourselves. It is also the call to assembly that the prophets used before a fast (Joel 2:16). The book began with the LORD's "gathering" to end everything (1:2); here the people are told to gather themselves first.

p: Chaff, the husk the wind blows off grain, is the Bible's picture of what does not last.
b: At the threshing floor, grain was tossed in the air and the wind carried off the light husk, the chaff. Psalm 1:4 says the wicked are like chaff the wind blows away. Hosea 13:3 and Isaiah 17:13 use the same picture of the people who will vanish. Here the day itself passes like chaff: the time left to turn back is short. The sentence is not easy Hebrew (see the variant), but the sense, that time is running out, is clear.

a: All you humble people of the land
p: The Hebrew 'anawim: people who are humble before God, often poor and pushed aside.
b: 'Anawim, "humble ones," are people who depend on God. The word is near to 'aniyyim, "the afflicted, the poor" (3:12), and the two roots mix in the Bible. Moses is called 'anav (Numbers 12:3). Psalm 37:11 says the humble will inherit the land. Zephaniah 2:3 gives the humble three things to do: seek the LORD, seek righteousness, seek humility. Scholars since the 1890s (Rahlfs, 1892; later Gelin, 1953) have written of a group of "the poor of the LORD," the anawim. Whether they were a party is debated; the text speaks of a spirit, not an organization. See the topic page.

p: Chapter 1 named those who do not seek; chapter 2 asks everyone to; Amos 5:14-15 is the nearest parallel.
b: Amos 5:4-6 says to seek the LORD and live and, a few verses later, to seek good and not evil, so that perhaps the LORD will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph (Amos 5:14-15). Zephaniah 2:3 repeats that shape: seek, and "perhaps." The triple "seek" is also an answer to 1:6, the people who had not sought him. Seeking righteousness and humility is not a way to earn escape; it is the way the humble show they are the LORD's. Whether they will be spared is left in God's hands (see the next note).

p: "Perhaps" leaves room for God's freedom; "hidden" may echo the prophet's own name.
b: 'Ulay, "perhaps," is the prophets' word for God's freedom: nobody can force his hand (Amos 5:15). Joel 2:14 and Jonah 3:9 say the same thing with "who knows?" (mi yode'a). The verb "be hidden" is sathar. The prophet's own name, Zephaniah, comes from tsafan, "to hide, treasure," a near-synonym (Psalm 27:5 uses both, "he will hide me... he will conceal me"). Some commentators hear a play on his name: "perhaps you will be Zephaniah, hidden by the LORD." The text does not point to the name, so this is a possible echo, not a claim. Even so, the verse offers no guarantee: it offers a chance.

p: Gaza's name sounds like "abandoned" and Ekron's like "uprooted"; Ashdod and Ashkelon are named between.
b: The Hebrew has plays on sound. 'Azzah 'azuvah: "Gaza, abandoned." 'Eqron te'aqer: "Ekron will be rooted out." The English cannot keep the first sound-play; the Plain keeps the second. The fifth Philistine city, Gath, is not named (as in Amos 1:6-8, Jeremiah 25:20, Zechariah 9:5-6), perhaps because Gath had already fallen (2 Kings 12:17; Amos 6:2). Gaza was taken by Pharaoh (Jeremiah 47:1; Herodotus mentions Necho taking a great city of Syria, Kadytis, often identified with Gaza).
orig: עַזָּה עֲזוּבָה ... וְעֶקְרוֹן תֵּעָקֵר ('azzah 'azuvah ... ve'eqron te'aqer)

a: At noon they will drive Ashdod out
p: Ashdod withstood a 29-year siege by Egypt in this century; "at noon" means an open, daylight attack.
b: Herodotus says the Egyptian king Psammetichus besieged Ashdod for twenty-nine years, longer than any other city, until it fell (Histories 2.157). Noon was a time of rest; an attack "at noon" was a surprise (Jeremiah 6:4, "attack at noon"; Jeremiah 15:8). Zephaniah gives the date of the vision no more precisely than this. The Philistines faced Egypt, then Babylon, within a lifetime.

p: A Babylonian army destroyed Ashkelon in 604 BC; a burned level has been dug there.
b: The Babylonian Chronicle records that in the month of Kislev in Nebuchadnezzar's first year (604 BC) he marched to Ashkelon, took its king and plundered the city. The Chronicle says he turned it into a mound and heaps of ruins. The excavators of Ashkelon (Lawrence Stager's team) report a thick burned layer of that date. This is one of the few places where a prophet's words and the dig line up closely. It does not prove Zephaniah's words were written before the event, as the burning could have been seen as the fulfillment afterward.

p: Another name for people of the Philistine coast, perhaps linked to Crete; David's bodyguard had Kerethites.
b: The Kerethites are known from 1 Samuel 30:14 (a raid on the Negev of the Kerethites) and Ezekiel 25:16. David's bodyguard was made up of the Kerethites and the Pelethites (2 Samuel 8:18), and Pelethites is probably another form of "Philistines." The name sounds like Crete, and some link them, but that is a guess (Hebrew Kaphtor is the Philistine home in Amos 9:7). The Greek here reads "neighbors of the Cretans" and in 2:6 "Crete." The Plain keeps the Hebrew name Kerethites.

a: what is left of the house of Judah
p: The remnant of Judah graze on the Philistine coast; some link it with Josiah's time, others with the future.
b: "What is left of the house of Judah" is the remnant theme (see 3:12-13). The picture is of shepherds taking over the pastures of the coast, which Isaiah 11:14 puts as Judah swooping on the Philistine slopes. Was this fulfilled? Some point to Josiah's reach toward the coast, and to a Hebrew letter on a potsherd from Mesad Hashavyahu, a fort on the coast near Yavneh-Yam from the late 600s BC, as evidence of a Judean presence (its ownership is debated: Judah or Egypt). Others see no event and read the verse as a promise for the future.

p: Insults against Judah by Moab and Ammon fit many times; the dating of this passage is part of the debate.
b: Moab and Ammon were Judah's kin, descended from Lot (Genesis 19:37-38), and old rivals. Their insults are recorded for the fall of Jerusalem: Ammon rejoiced (Ezekiel 25:3, 6), Moab said Judah was like every other nation (Ezekiel 25:8), and bands of Moabites and Ammonites raided Judah under Jehoiakim (2 Kings 24:2). If these are the insults meant, 2:8-11 may be later than Josiah's day, which is one reason some critics think the passage was added after 598 or 586. Defenders of Zephaniah's authorship point out that Moab and Ammon taunted Israel for centuries (Judges 3; Judges 11; Isaiah 16; Jeremiah 48:27).

p: YHWH tseva'ot: the LORD with the armies of heaven and earth under his command.
b: YHWH tseva'ot, "the LORD of Armies," appears first in 1 Samuel 1:3 and often in the prophets. The "armies" may be Israel's own armies, the angels or the stars (compare "the army of the heavens" in 1:5). The Greek writes Kyrios pantokrator, "the Lord, ruler of all" (the Greek at 2:10). The title says that those who bow to the "army of the heavens" in 1:5 are bowing to his servants. This verse also gives God's oath "as I live," an oath sworn on his own life.

t: Sodom, Gomorrah and the children of Lot
p: Moab and Ammon are the children of Lot, who escaped Sodom; now they share its fate.
b: Sodom and Gomorrah are the standing example of a land the LORD wiped out (Genesis 19:24-25; Deuteronomy 29:23; Isaiah 13:19; Amos 4:11). Moab and Ammon trace their ancestry to the daughters of Lot, who escaped from Sodom (Genesis 19:30-38). The prophet's words bring them back to their origin: the sons of the survivor share the doom of the city. Salt and nettles belong to the picture, as in Deuteronomy 29:23, the land of "brimstone and salt." In the Greek of this verse the name Damascus appears (see the variant).

a: What is left of my people will plunder them
p: The remnant of Judah takes over the lands of its enemies; Isaiah 11:14 and Obadiah say the same.
b: The "remnant" and "survivors" are the same people as in 3:12-13. Isaiah 11:14 pictures Judah swooping on the Philistines and taking Edom, Moab and Ammon; Obadiah 19-21 pictures the same for Edom. The promise reverses Moab and Ammon's insults against the LORD's people (2:8). Some readers see this fulfilled in the Hasmonean conquests of the 100s BC; others place it with the last days.

a: make all the gods of the earth waste away
p: The Hebrew means to make lean or thin: the gods are not destroyed by fire, but wasted by want.
b: The verb razah means "to be lean, to waste away" (Isaiah 17:4 uses the same verb for the fat of Jacob's flesh growing lean). Gods lived by being fed with offerings; they weaken when their worshipers turn away. The prophets mock this (Isaiah 44:9-20; Jeremiah 10:1-16). The Greek says the LORD will "utterly destroy" them. Their gods wasted, the nations turn: "everyone will bow down to him from their own place." That is a picture of worship all over the earth, not only on Zion (compare Malachi 1:11).
orig: כִּי רָזָה אֵת כָּל־אֱלֹהֵי הָאָרֶץ (ki razah et kol-elohe ha'arets)

a: all the coastlands of the nations
p: The distant lands across the sea; Genesis 10:5 uses the same phrase for the nations that spread from Noah's sons.
b: 'Iyyei hagoyim is "the coastlands of the nations," the very words of Genesis 10:5 for the peoples descended from Japheth who spread around the Mediterranean. For Judah the coastlands were the far west, the end of the known world. Isaiah 42:4 says the coastlands wait for his teaching, and Isaiah 66:19 sends survivors to the distant coastlands that have not heard of his fame. Zephaniah's picture is the same: even the farthest peoples bow.

p: Cush, or Nubia, lay south of Egypt; the verse completes a map of the four directions.
b: Cush (Nubia, south of Egypt) was the far south. The Cushite kings had ruled Egypt as the 25th dynasty until Assyria drove them out in the 660s BC. Many commentators note that Zephaniah names a nation at each point of the compass: the Philistines on the west (2:4-7), Moab and Ammon on the east (2:8-11), Cush on the south (2:12) and Assyria on the north (2:13-15). So the Cushites may stand for the whole south, including Egypt. The prophet's own father had a Cushite name (1:1), and in 3:10 Cush sends worshipers. The same people who are slain by the sword are later pictured bringing offerings.

p: Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC; this is also the subject of Nahum's whole book.
b: The Babylonian Chronicle records that Babylonians and Medes took Nineveh in the summer of 612 BC, and that Ashur-uballit II held out at Harran until about 609. In Josiah's early years Assyria was still the master of the region; if Zephaniah spoke then, this was a bold word. The same fall is the subject of Nahum (see the Plain of Nahum 2-3). Jonah's Nineveh, which repents and is spared, belongs to an earlier time (see the note on Nahum 3:7). Josiah died in 609 at Megiddo, going out against Pharaoh Neco who marched north to help the last of Assyria (2 Kings 23:29).

a: The desert owl and the hedgehog
p: Hebrew qa'at and qippod: the birds are uncertain; Isaiah 34:11 names the same pair for a ruined land.
b: The Hebrew has two creatures of ruins. Qa'at is an unclean bird listed in Leviticus 11:18 and Deuteronomy 14:17 and in Psalm 102:6; it is perhaps a pelican, an owl or a bittern. Qippod is perhaps the hedgehog or porcupine, or a kind of owl or bittern (Isaiah 14:23; 34:11). The Plain follows Isaiah 34:11, "desert owl" and "hedgehog." The Greek has "chameleons and hedgehogs." The point is the same in each reading: wild creatures where kings once sat.

p: The Hebrew kaftor means the top of a column, or a knob; the Greek reads "vaulted ceilings."
b: Kaftor is the knob or capital at the top of a column. It is used for the knobs on the lampstand (Exodus 25:31-36) and for the capitals Amos sees struck in the temple (Amos 9:1). Birds nest on carved column-tops in a ruined palace. The Plain says "the tops of its pillars." Bird or beast: whichever one it is, the lodger has replaced the king.

a: From the window comes a singing voice
p: A bird sings from the window of a palace that has no one left; the image is of silence broken only by animals.
b: In a living house a window shows the family. Here the voice at the window is a bird or the wind, and the house has nobody. The verb yeshorer is "sing," usually said of people; here it is the empty building that sings. Isaiah 34:11-15 gives the same picture of Edom, with owls, ravens, jackals and kites living in the ruin.

a: "I am, and besides me there is nothing."
p: Nineveh says what Babylon says in Isaiah 47: nothing but me. Isaiah and Ezekiel call the same pride.
b: The phrase "I am, and besides me there is nothing" (Isaiah 47:8) is what Babylon says in Isaiah, and again in Isaiah 47:10; here Nineveh says it. In Ezekiel 28:2 the ruler of Tyre says "I am a god." The words claim for a city what belongs to God alone (Isaiah 45:5-6). The Hebrew is the same in both books ('ani ve'afsi 'od); Zephaniah turns Babylon's boast against Nineveh. The empire's boast is the sin the empire is punished for. Nineveh's other face is in Jonah, where the same city repents.

p: Hissing and the waving hand are signs of scorn at a ruin; Jeremiah and Lamentations have the same.
b: To "hiss" (whistle) at a ruined city was a sign of horror or contempt (Jeremiah 19:8; 49:17; Lamentations 2:15). The hand "waved" may be a shake of the head and hand to show scorn or a gesture of dismissal; Nahum 3:19 says the people all clap their hands at the fall of Nineveh. The same two gestures are used of Jerusalem in Lamentations 2:15, so the scorn Nineveh gets here is what Jerusalem will later endure.

p: The Hebrew can be read "the oppressing" (yanah) or "the dove" (yonah); the Greek and Latin read "dove."
b: Hayyonah can come from yanah, "to oppress" (as in "the oppressing sword," Jeremiah 46:16; 50:16), which is how the pointed Hebrew text and most modern versions read it. It can also be yonah, "dove," which is how the Greek (peristera) and Jerome's Latin (columba) read it. Hosea 7:11 calls Ephraim a silly dove. A dove city would be one that was gentle but silly, or beloved. The Plain follows the Hebrew with "oppressing"; the next verses say what she has done.

p: The city is not named; nearly all commentators say Jerusalem.
b: Zephaniah does not name this city. Nearly all readers take it as Jerusalem, because the next verses speak of the LORD in her midst, her prophets and her priests (3:4-5). The section follows the oracle against Nineveh closely, and in Swete's Greek the verse numbering puts 2:15 at the start of its chapter 3. That is an editors' numbering and does not show that anyone read 3:1 as Nineveh. The Hebrew shift from "woe" (hoy) to a charge against the leaders makes Jerusalem much likelier. The site's term for hoy is "Woe to," the cry used at funerals.

p: Four "nots" sum up the failure: she did not listen, learn, trust or come near.
b: The four charges echo Jeremiah. Jeremiah 7:28 says the people did not listen to the LORD's voice and did not accept correction; Jeremiah 5:3 says they refused to take correction; 2:30 says they did not learn the lesson. The word is musar, "correction, discipline": the training a parent or teacher gives, including punishment. Four negatives in a row (voice, correction, trust, nearness) leave nothing positive to say. Jeremiah was preaching in the same streets in the same decades.

p: Leaders who eat the people: lions and wolves appear in Ezekiel, Micah and Habakkuk.
b: The image of rulers as predators is old. Ezekiel 22:25 compares the princes of Jerusalem to a roaring lion tearing its prey, and Ezekiel 22:27 compares the officials to wolves tearing prey. Proverbs 28:15 does the same for a wicked ruler. Micah 3:1-3 has the rulers eating the people's flesh. "Evening wolves" appears again in Habakkuk 1:8, for the Babylonian horsemen. The Greek reads "wolves of Arabia," taking the Hebrew word for evening ('erev) as Arabia ('arav), and Jeremiah 5:6 has "a wolf from the desert plains."
r: Ezekiel 22:25; Ezekiel 22:27; Proverbs 28:15; Micah 3:1-3; Habakkuk 1:8; Jeremiah 5:6

p: The Hebrew pochazim is used of water that foams over and of lawless men; the Greek reads "carried by a spirit."
b: Pochaz is used of Reuben as "boiling over like water" (Genesis 49:4) and of the reckless men Abimelech hired (Judges 9:4). It means unstable, lacking control. The Greek calls the prophets pneumatophoroi, "spirit-carried," the word it also uses in Hosea 9:7 for the "man of the spirit." The prophets of 3:4 are false because they speak out of their own loose impulse. Jeremiah 23, Micah 3:5-8 and Lamentations 4:13 charge Judah's prophets and priests together.
r: Genesis 49:4; Judges 9:4; Hosea 9:7; Jeremiah 23:9-32; Micah 3:5-8; Lamentations 4:13

a: treat what is holy as common
p: The line is close to Ezekiel 22:26, which blames priests for blurring holy and common.
b: Priests were set to teach the difference between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean (Leviticus 10:10-11). Ezekiel 22:26 charges that the priests of his day "have done violence to my law and profaned what is holy to me." Zephaniah's charge has the same two parts: they treat the holy as common, and they do violence to the law. Haggai 2:11-13 shows what priests were asked to rule on. The failure is not ignorance but misuse.

p: Torah can be "law" or "teaching"; here it is the priests' instruction and judgment.
b: Torah means teaching, instruction. In the prophets it often means what the priests taught and judged (Jeremiah 2:8; Malachi 2:6-7; Haggai 2:11), and the Plain gives "law" as in Ezekiel 22:26 and Jeremiah 2:8, with this note. Chamas, "violence," is a strong word, used of bloodshed and of the sin that filled the earth before the flood (Genesis 6:11). The priests wrong the law by twisting it, as a violent man twists an arm.

p: The same Hebrew phrase links the book's last chapter: the officials, the LORD, the humble and the King are each "in her midst."
b: Beqirbah, "in her midst," is a refrain of chapter 3. Her officials are lions "in her midst" (3:3). The LORD is righteous "in her midst" (3:5). He will remove the proud "from your midst" (3:11). He will leave a humble people "in your midst" (3:12). The LORD, the King of Israel, is "in your midst" (3:15), and again (3:17). The chapter is a contest over who stands at the center of the city, and the last verses answer.

a: Morning after morning he brings his justice to the light
p: A judge sat at dawn in the gate; God's justice is as regular as sunrise.
b: In the ancient world justice was done in the morning, in the open, at the city gate. Jeremiah 21:12 tells the house of David to give justice in the morning, and Psalm 101:8 has the king silencing the wicked "every morning." Hosea 6:5 says the LORD's judgment goes out like light. Zephaniah says God does this every morning and never fails. The leaders in 3:3 eat the poor before the morning; the LORD acts in the light.

p: In Mesopotamia the sun god Shamash was the god of justice, who brought wrongs to light.
b: In Mesopotamian religion the sun god Shamash was the judge: the top of Hammurabi's law stele shows Shamash handing the king the symbols of justice. A god of the sun who sees every deed is a natural god of the courts. Zephaniah's picture of the LORD bringing justice "to the light" every morning fits that world of images, and in Judah, where sun worship was a live temptation (2 Kings 23:5, 11), it makes a claim: justice comes from the LORD, not from the sun. There is no proof of direct borrowing. The verdict is a shared picture, not a source.

p: "Shame" is a word that comes up again in 3:11, 3:19 and 3:20; the book moves from no shame to no more shame.
b: Bosheth is shame: public disgrace as well as the feeling of it. The wrongdoer "knows no shame" (3:5), has no sense that he is disgraced. In 3:11 the LORD's people "will not be ashamed" of their deeds, because he removes the proud. In 3:19-20 the scattered are shamed in every land where they were put to shame, and the LORD turns that shame into praise and a name. The book follows the word from shamelessness to shame to restored honor.

p: The LORD points to nations he has already ruined as a warning to Jerusalem.
b: The Hebrew has a perfect tense: "I have cut off nations." Past judgments are meant as a warning, as in the story of Judah's neighbors and the northern kingdom (2 Kings 17; Jeremiah 3:6-10). The Greek speaks of "the proud ones" instead of "nations." The "corner towers" lying in ruins are the same word as in 1:16. A city is told to learn from the cities it has seen die. The sentence does not name the nations; Samaria and the northern kingdom are the nearest example.

p: In Jeremiah God rises early to send prophets; here the people rise early to do wrong.
b: "Rising early" is a Hebrew way to say "eagerly, persistently." In Jeremiah the LORD says again and again that he "rose early and sent" his servants the prophets (Jeremiah 7:13, 25; 25:3-4; 35:15). Zephaniah turns it around: the people "got up early" to spoil everything they did. God was eager to save; they were eager to ruin. The Greek ends this verse differently: "Get ready, rise early, all their gleanings are ruined."

p: The LORD tells the faithful to wait for him, the verb of Habakkuk 2:3 and Isaiah 30:18.
b: Chakkeh, "wait," is the verb of hope. Habakkuk 2:3 uses it for waiting for the vision, "wait for it," and Isaiah 30:18 calls blessed everyone who waits for him. Here the LORD says it of himself: wait for me. The wait is not for rescue only; it is for "the day I rise up," a day that will hit the nations. The word "therefore" at the start joins the verse to the failures of 3:1-7: because the city will not learn, the answer is to wait for God's own action.

p: The Greek and Latin read "the day of my resurrection," which Christian readers have heard as Christ's rising.
b: The Hebrew says "the day I rise up" (qumi), as a judge or a warrior rises to act (Psalm 12:5; Isaiah 33:10). The Greek has anastaseos mou, "my resurrection," and the Latin resurrectionis meae, which Christian commentators in those languages connected with Christ's rising on the third day. The Hebrew does not say this and the Plain does not follow the Greek here. It is the church's reading of the Greek and Latin words, not what Zephaniah's own sentence says.

a: I will gather nations and assemble kingdoms
p: The LORD gathers the nations for judgment: the verb 'asaf is the one that opened the book.
b: The picture of the LORD gathering the nations to judge them is also in Joel 3:2 (the valley of Jehoshaphat) and Zechariah 14:2. The verb is 'asaf, the same as in 1:2, "I will bring everything to an end," and as in 3:18-20, where the LORD gathers the scattered. Here the first use is for nations to be judged; later uses are for the scattered to be rescued. The Plain uses "gather" for the nations and "end" for 1:2 because of the sense, with the note on 1:2 on the double sound.

p: Hebrew has many words for anger; the Plain keeps them apart: za'am "indignation," charon 'af "burning anger."
b: Za'am, "indignation," is anger poured out (Psalm 69:24; Isaiah 26:20); charon 'af, "burning anger," is anger that flares (2:2; Exodus 32:12). The verse piles them: indignation, all the heat of burning anger, the fire of jealousy. The pile ends the oracles on the nations as 1:18 ended the oracle on Judah. For the whole group of words and what they mean, see the topic wrath.

a: change the lips of the peoples
p: In Hebrew "lip" can mean language; the same word is used for "one language" in Genesis 11.
b: Safah, "lip," is also "language." Genesis 11:1 says all the earth had "one lip" before Babel, and Genesis 11:7-9 says the LORD confused their lips. Zephaniah 3:9 uses the same word: God will "turn" (change) the peoples' lips into pure ones. What is "pure"? Two readings. (1) Cleansed speech: lips that no longer name idols (Hosea 2:17; Psalm 16:4) or that are cleansed like Isaiah's (Isaiah 6:5-7). (2) One speech again, a reversal of Babel. The next clause, "so that all of them call on the name of the LORD," fits both.

p: The church reads the pure lips with Acts 2: at Pentecost many languages praise the LORD together.
b: Christians have read this verse beside Acts 2, where the Spirit comes and people from every nation hear the praise of God in their own languages (Acts 2:1-11). Babel scattered the peoples by confusing their speech; Pentecost gathers them without erasing their languages. The Kontakion of Pentecost in the Byzantine rite makes this link: it says that when the Most High came down and confused the tongues he divided the nations, but when he gave out the tongues of fire he called all to unity. This is the church's reading, an echo of Zephaniah 3:9 rather than a quotation of it, and the New Testament does not cite the verse.

a: so that all of them call on the name of the LORD
p: Joel 2:32, quoted in Acts 2:21 and Romans 10:13, uses the same words.
b: To "call on the name of the LORD" is the old phrase for worship (Genesis 4:26; Psalm 116:13). Joel 2:32 promises that everyone who calls on the name will be saved, and Peter quotes it at Pentecost (Acts 2:21) and Paul in Romans 10:13. Zephaniah's promise is the same in its reach: "all of them," from every people. The verse is the book's turn from the judgment of the nations to their conversion.

p: Hebrew has "with one shoulder," pictured as people bearing a load together.
b: The Hebrew is shekhem 'ehad, "one shoulder." Shekhem is the shoulder, the part of the body that carries a load (Genesis 49:15, Issachar "bent his shoulder to the load"). Peoples serving with one shoulder are like oxen under a single yoke, or workers lifting the same weight. The Greek reads "under one yoke." The Plain's "side by side" gives the meaning, with the shoulder in the gloss. Serving the LORD becomes a team job for the nations.

a: from beyond the rivers of Cush
p: The far south: Isaiah 18:1 uses these words; Christians have linked the verse with the Ethiopian official of Acts 8.
b: "Beyond the rivers of Cush" are the words of Isaiah 18:1 for the land beyond the Nile and its branches in Nubia, the far end of the known south. The verse says worshipers will bring offerings from there. Psalm 68:31 says Cush will stretch out its hands to God, and Isaiah 66:20 says the nations will bring your relatives as an offering. Some Christian readers have linked the verse with the Ethiopian official of Acts 8:27-39, who traveled from the court of the queen of the Cushites to worship in Jerusalem. That link is the church's reading.

a: the daughter of my scattered ones
p: Foreign worshipers or scattered Jews: the grammar of this verse allows both.
b: The Hebrew has three nouns in a row: "my worshipers, daughter of my scattered ones, will bring my offering." Two readings. (1) The worshipers are Judeans scattered as far as Cush, and they bring an offering home (Isaiah 11:11; Elephantine in Egypt had a Jewish colony). (2) They are people of Cush, foreigners who worship the LORD and bring offerings, and "daughter of my scattered ones" names them as part of the people God scatters among the nations (Isaiah 18:7; 66:20 is a related picture). The Greek reads "I will accept my scattered ones from the ends of the rivers of Cush; they will bring sacrifices to me."

a: those who revel in your pride
p: The root 'alaz appears in 2:15 (exulted), 3:11 (revel) and 3:14 (celebrate): proud joy turns into true joy.
b: 'Alaz means to exult. In 2:15 Nineveh is ha'alizah, the "exulting" city. In 3:11 the proud in Jerusalem are 'alizei ga'avatekh, "those who revel in your pride." And in 3:14 the daughter of Jerusalem is told ve'alzi, "celebrate." One root, three meanings: the empire's exulting, the proud's exulting, and the humble's exulting. The Plain uses three English words ("exulted," "revel," "celebrate") so each fits its context. The book moves from exulting in pride to exulting in the LORD.

p: The Hebrew 'ani and dal: afflicted, lowly; the Greek says "gentle and humble."
b: 'Ani means afflicted, bowed down, and so humble; dal means weak, poor, low. They are the people who, in 2:3, are the 'anawim. The Plain uses "humble" for 'anav (2:3) and "afflicted" for 'ani (3:12) so the two stay distinct. The Greek reads praun kai tapeinon, "gentle and lowly." The first word is the one used for "the meek" in the Greek Psalm 37:11 and in the Beatitude of Matthew 5:5, so the Greek reader hears a link. Matthew 5:3-5 and Luke 6:20 echo this kind of people without quoting the verse. See the topic page.

a: I will leave in your midst
p: In Zephaniah the survivors are not the strong but the poor who trust God; Paul uses the remnant idea in Romans.
b: The Hebrew verb hish'arti, "I will leave," comes from the same root as she'erit, "remnant" (3:13). The survivors of the day of the LORD are not the rich and powerful whose silver cannot rescue them (1:18), but the afflicted and poor who "take refuge in the name of the LORD." Paul uses the remnant idea in Romans 9:27 and 11:5. Whether a specific group or a spirit is meant, Zephaniah ties survival to trust, not to status.

p: The verb chasah is the Psalms' word for running to God for shelter.
b: Chasah, "take refuge," is the Psalter's word for turning to God as a shelter (Psalm 2:12; 34:8; 37:40). It is the opposite of trusting in silver and gold (1:18). The people who survive will be those who have done what Psalm 2:12 recommends.

p: "Israel" here is Jerusalem's people; the church and Jewish readers read the remnant differently.
b: In Zephaniah "the remnant of Israel" is the humble people left in Jerusalem after judgment, who live in justice and truth. Jewish readers take the promise as for the Jewish people, restored after exile. Christians have read the remnant as the true Israel, in which Jew and Gentile are joined, as in Romans 9-11. Others, including Messianic Jewish and Dispensationalist readers, keep it distinct for Israel's own future. The words say only that this remnant does no wrong and speaks no lies, and rests undisturbed.

p: Isaiah 53:9 and Revelation 14:5 have the same mark of the faithful: no deceit found in the mouth.
b: Isaiah 53:9 says of the servant that no deceit was in his mouth. Revelation 14:5 says no lie was found in the mouths of the 144,000 who follow the Lamb. Both lines may echo Zephaniah, who says no deceitful tongue will be found in the mouths of the remnant. Whether Revelation draws on Zephaniah directly is the church's reading; it is a possible echo only. The pure lips of 3:9 lead to the honest lips of 3:13.

a: They will graze and lie down
p: The remnant lies down in safety like a flock; 2:7 used the same verbs for Judah on the coast.
b: "Graze and lie down" are the verbs of a flock at peace. They were used in 2:7 of Judah's remnant on the Philistine coast. Psalm 23:2 has the shepherd making the sheep lie down in green pastures; Ezekiel 34:13-15, 28 and Micah 4:4 have the same picture of safe pasture, with no one to frighten them. Leviticus 26:6 promised it as a blessing. The humble people who run to the LORD are his flock.

p: Zion's people as a daughter: the city is a person, the one who wept in laments and now cries out for joy.
b: Bat Tsiyyon, "Daughter Zion," is the city or its people spoken of as a young woman. Lamentations uses it for the weeping city. Here the same figure is told to cry out for joy. Zechariah 9:9 uses the same words for the call to joy at the coming of the king, and John 12:15 quotes them at Jesus' entry into Jerusalem. "Daughter Jerusalem" is the same figure with the other name. The Plain keeps the site's term "Daughter Zion."

t: The war-cry becomes a shout of joy
p: The same Hebrew root that gave the battle cry in 1:16 gives the shout of joy here.
b: Hari'u, "raise a shout," comes from rua', the root of teru'ah, the "battle cry" of 1:16. The shout that came against the fortified cities is now the shout of the people. In the same way the "warrior" who shouted in 1:14 is the warrior who rescues in 3:17. The book builds an answer to its own first half: the sounds of the day of the LORD return as the sounds of the day of rescue. Joy is not the opposite of the judgment; it is the same sounds with a new meaning.

p: The Hebrew mishpatayikh: the verdicts or punishments against her; the Greek reads "your wrongs."
b: Mishpat is the word for justice, a ruling, a judgment. "Your judgments" here are the sentences passed against Jerusalem. To take them away is to cancel the verdict. The Greek reads adikemata sou, "your wrongs," which makes the verse a pardon. The Plain keeps "judgments," which allows both: the punishments are lifted. Compare Isaiah 40:2, where her penalty has been paid.

p: God is the king in her midst; the same title was acclaimed at Jesus' entry into Jerusalem.
b: The title "King of Israel" for the LORD is in Isaiah 44:6; here it replaces the human king, who is not mentioned in the promise of rescue (compare Zephaniah 1:8, where the royal house is judged). John 12:13 has the crowd call Jesus "the King of Israel," and John 12:15 puts the words "Do not be afraid, Daughter Zion" before Zechariah 9:9. Commentators think John joins Zechariah 9:9 to the call not to fear (Zephaniah 3:16 or Isaiah 40:9). The Christian reading is that the King who dwells in her midst has come in person.

p: "Do not fear, Zion" is the voice of the prophets' consolation; it sits in John 12:15.
b: "Do not be afraid" is the standard word of the LORD's help (Isaiah 41:10; 43:1). In Isaiah 40:9 Zion is told to lift up her voice and not fear. John 12:15 starts with "Do not be afraid, Daughter Zion," and then quotes Zechariah 9:9. Scholars note that Zephaniah 3:16 and Isaiah 40:9 are the likeliest sources of the opening words. "Let your hands not go slack" is the language of courage: in Isaiah 35:3 the weak hands are strengthened.

p: Gibbor, the warrior, is the word of 1:14; now he fights for her, as in Exodus 15:3.
b: The same word gibbor that described a warrior shouting in defeat on the day of the LORD (1:14) now describes the LORD himself as the warrior who rescues. Exodus 15:3 says the LORD is a warrior. Isaiah 42:13 says he goes out like a warrior. The Greek has ho dynatos sosei se, "the mighty one will save you." The war image that frightened in chapter 1 now comforts: the warrior is on her side.

a: He will cheer over you with a ringing shout.
t: The LORD rejoicing aloud over his people
p: The Hebrew has the LORD himself rejoicing over Zion with a ringing cry (rinnah); the root can mean a shout or a song.
b: The picture is of the LORD rejoicing over his people with a loud cry, the way a bridegroom or a victor rejoices (Isaiah 62:5). The root ranan covers a ringing cry of joy and a song of joy: Psalm 33:1 uses it for "sing for joy." The Plain uses "ringing cry" and "ringing shout" for it here and in 3:14, and so does not say "sing"; a reader who hears song in the Hebrew is on firm ground, but the Plain does not claim it. The Greek has no cry at all: the LORD will rejoice over her "as on a feast day." Readers have seen the line as God's joy at the end of exile. Some Catholic readers connect the passage with Mary (see the card). Whatever the reading, the picture is rare in the Bible: God does not only save but cries out for joy over his people. See the variant on the previous line.

a: The LORD your God is in your midst
p: In the Greek, 3:14-17 shares the word "Rejoice" with Gabriel's greeting in Luke 1; this is the church's reading.
b: The Greek of Zephaniah 3:14 begins Chaire, "Rejoice," the same word as Gabriel's first word to Mary (Luke 1:28). That is the one exact Greek link, and chaire is common elsewhere (Zechariah 9:9 in the Greek has it). The other links are weaker. Luke 1:30, "Do not be afraid" (me phobou), matches the sense of the Hebrew of Zephaniah 3:16 ('al tira'i), but the Greek of 3:16 reads Tharsei, Seion, "Take courage, Zion," not "do not be afraid." The Greek of Zephaniah 3:15 and 3:17 says the Lord is "in your midst" (en meso sou) and "in you" (en soi), while Luke 1:28 says "the Lord is with you" (meta sou), a different phrase. Catholic teaching calls Mary the "Daughter of Sion" (Lumen Gentium 55), but that passage does not cite Zephaniah; its footnotes cite Genesis 3:15, Isaiah 7:14, Micah 5:2-3 and Matthew 1:22-23. The Roman lectionary does join the two: Zephaniah 3:14-18 is read on the Third Sunday of Advent in Year C and may be read at the feast of the Visitation (31 May). Whether Luke meant the echo is debated. See the card.

t: The hardest verse in the book
p: The Hebrew of 3:18 is broken; the translation is a best guess and the Greek reads something quite different.
b: The Hebrew has five phrases with no clear grammar. "Those who grieve" (nugei) are from a root meaning to grieve, or, in another reading, to be driven away. "From the appointed feast" (mimmo'ed) may mean grieving over the missed festivals, or removed from them. "I will gather" ('asafti, literally "I have gathered") is the same verb as 1:2. "They were yours" and "the reproach on her was a burden" end the verse. The Plain gives the best sense: the LORD will gather those who mourned the lost festivals (Lamentations 1:4; Josiah's Passover in 2 Kings 23:21-23 reminds us what was at stake). The Greek reads "I will gather the crushed. Woe: who took reproach on her?" See the variant.

a: gather those who were driven away
t: Claude's theory: the book is bracketed by one verb
p: Spec: the book may be framed by the verb 'asaf, "gather," used first to end the world and last to bring people home.
b: This is Claude's own observation, not a settled view. The Hebrew verb 'asaf opens the book twice ("I will gather... everything" in 1:2-3, the pun on gathering and ending) and returns as the book's last act: the LORD "gathers" the nations to judge them (3:8), then "gathers" the grieving, the lame and the outcast (3:18-20; the word for gather in 3:19-20 is qibbets, a sibling verb). Taken together the verb marks the book's turn. The same God does the gathering in both halves. Commentators have noted the wordplay in 1:2 and the closing gathering, but I have not seen the single-verb frame argued in this form. The reading rests on 1:2-3, 3:8, 3:18-20.

a: I will make them a praise and a name
p: Deuteronomy 26:19 and Jeremiah 13:11 use the same three words; the shamed become honored.
b: "Praise and a name" (tehillah veshem) repeats the language of Israel's calling in Deuteronomy 26:19, where the LORD sets his people high "in praise, in name and in honor." Jeremiah 13:11 uses it of the people as a belt the LORD wanted to wear, which they refused to be. Zephaniah says the promise will come true in the land where they were shamed (3:19) and among all peoples (3:20): the place of shame becomes the place of honor.

p: Shuv shevut, "turn (someone's) fortunes around": used of Job and of Judah after exile.
b: The idiom shuv shevut is used of the end of a time of loss, as for Job (Job 42:10) and for Judah and Israel in Jeremiah (Jeremiah 29:14; 30:3; 33:7, 11). The site's term is "turn fortunes around." Whether the noun is shevut "fortune" or shevit "captivity" is a spelling question in the Hebrew texts (see the variant at 2:7), and the Greek translates "captivity." The idiom is used of exile, but is not limited to it.

a: At that time I will bring you in
t: Who is brought in, and when?
p: Return from Babylon, an ongoing gathering, or the last days: readers differ on what "bring you in" means.
b: The promise of gathering and bringing in has been read several ways. (1) The return from Babylon (after 538 BC), if the passage was written or added during or after the exile; the phrase "turn your fortunes around" fits a people in exile. (2) Josiah's day, if it is a hope tied to the reform and the call to northern Israel, which was already scattered. (3) The church: the gathering of the scattered into one people through Christ (compare John 11:51-52). (4) The last days, when Israel and the nations are gathered together. The Plain gives the words, and the chapter note gives these four.
